section_summary: This section contains U.S. diplomatic correspondence, State Department memoranda, and intelligence reports from late 1933 and early 1934 regarding Japanese domestic politics and foreign policy. It documents the decline of parliamentary government, military influence, political scandals, and factional friction surrounding the Saito Cabinet and War Minister Araki's resignation. It also covers international concerns regarding Pan-Asiatic expansionism, the anticipated 1935 naval crisis, Soviet-Japanese border tensions, and the trials and imperial amnesty of civilian reactionaries in the May 15, 1932 incident.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew concludes his report analyzing Yosuke Matsuoka's resignation from the Seiyukai Party and the decline of parliamentary party government in Japan.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew evaluates the army's entrenched role in government and reactionary advocacy for direct imperial rule. He notes opinions that Japan may not yet be suited for Western parliamentary systems without stabilizing institutions like the Shogunate or Genro. He suggests Matsuoka's recent public statements reflect such perspectives.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 609: The Resignation of Mr. Matsuoka from the Seiyukai Party and the Unpopularity of Party Government in Japan (Conclusion)

subfiles.about: Duplicate copy and summary sheets of Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 609 discussing Yosuke Matsuoka's resignation and statement against party government.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The despatch details Yosuke Matsuoka's simultaneous resignation from the Seiyukai and the Diet and his denunciation of party politics as divisive. It explores widespread public distrust of politicians, the military's promotion of the Imperial Way, and historical mechanisms for national guidance. A summary cover sheet prefaces the despatch.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 609: The Resignation of Mr. Matsuoka from the Seiyukai Party and the Unpopularity of Party Government in Japan (Duplicate Copy and Summary)

subfiles.about: A memorandum and routing note recommending that Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 608 be brought to President Roosevelt's attention.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (BD / RY)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs suggests to Under Secretary Phillips that Tokyo Despatch No. 608 be brought to the notice of the President. An attached note records that the despatch was transmitted to President Roosevelt on January 15, 1934.
subfiles.title: Memorandum and Routing Note on Tokyo Despatch No. 608
subfiles.to: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the views of the Netherlands Minister reported in Tokyo Despatch No. 608.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (EHD / REK)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum outlines General Pabst's warnings regarding Japan's Pan-Asiatic aims, rising Japanese popularity in the East Indies, and potential naval strikes against Guam and the Philippines ahead of the 1935 naval talks. It reviews Grew's assessment of Foreign Minister Hirota's nationalist orientation and concurs that 1935 must be approached with caution.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Foreign Policies and Views of the Netherlands Minister

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports extensive conversations with Netherlands Minister General Pabst regarding Japanese Pan-Asiatic ambitions, naval strategy, and the anticipated 1935 crisis.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: General Pabst outlines Japan's Pan-Asiatic ambitions to organize Asia under its leadership and warns that the Japanese Navy might seize Guam and the Philippines if naval parity is refused in 1935. Pabst highlights military indifference to economic consequences and stresses threats to the Dutch East Indies. Grew considers Pabst a seasoned observer and urges vigilant attention to 1935.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 608: Political Problems in the Far East - Japanese Activities

subfiles.about: Under Secretary Phillips transmits a copy of Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 608 to President Roosevelt.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Phillips sends President Roosevelt Ambassador Grew's confidential despatch presenting the views of Netherlands Minister General Pabst. He notes with interest how closely General Pabst's assessments coincide with the Department's own views.
subfiles.title: Letter from Under Secretary Phillips to President Roosevelt Transmitting Despatch No. 608

subfiles.about: Acting Secretary Phillips acknowledges Grew's Despatch No. 608 and transmits a consular report on native politics in the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department commends Despatch No. 608 as highly informative regarding international relations in the Far East. It forwards for Grew's information a copy of a report dated November 14, 1933, from the American Consul General at Batavia regarding native politics.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 432 to Ambassador Grew Acknowledging Despatch No. 608
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: A document file note cross-referencing a report from Ambassador Grew regarding political unrest in Japan.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference sheet records Tokyo despatch 894.00 P.R./72 of December 11, 1933, reporting on political unrest in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00 P.R./72

subfiles.about: An extract reporting on anti-Saito Cabinet public demonstrations in Tokyo and the sentencing of civilian nationalist conspirators.
subfiles.summary: The report describes demonstrations by patriotic societies in Tokyo, including a massive rally in Shiba Park featuring Mitsuaki Tanaka demanding the resignation of the Saito Cabinet. It also reviews judicial deliberations and sentences for civilians involved in political violence, noting debates on judicial leniency for patriotic motives.
subfiles.title: Report Extract on Anti-Cabinet Demonstrations and Civilian Conspirator Sentences

subfiles.about: A letter from The Friendly Fellowship urging diplomatic efforts to prevent a Far Eastern war, enclosing an article by Upton Close.
subfiles.from: The Friendly Fellowship, Division of Practical Christianity (Chicago)
subfiles.summary: The sender urges Secretary Hull to counteract war consciousness between Japan and Russia. The enclosed article by Upton Close from the Chicago Herald and Examiner claims that Japan and Russia are actively preparing for war in spring 1934 and outlines military and strategic factors across Siberia and Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Letter from The Friendly Fellowship Transmitting Upton Close Newspaper Article

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum commenting on Tokyo Telegram No. 15 concerning General Araki's resignation as War Minister.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (EHD / REK)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum examines Ambassador Grew's telegram regarding Araki's resignation and Hayashi's appointment. It concludes that while major policy reversals are improbable, evidence supports the view that the leadership change favors moderation rather than reactionary escalation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Telegram No. 15 Regarding Resignation of War Minister Araki

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the resignation of War Minister Sadao Araki and evaluates hypotheses surrounding the appointment of General Senjuro Hayashi.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Grew analyzes theories regarding Araki's retirement, citing official illness, Cabinet isolation, and budget disputes with party leaders Suzuki and Wakatsuki. He assesses General Hayashi's reputation as a decisive field officer who opposes political activity by soldiers, suggesting the shift may stabilize domestic politics despite some concerns over his past actions in Korea.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 15: Resignation of War Minister Araki and Appointment of General Hayashi

subfiles.about: A document file note recording notes on Japan compiled by Francis P. Miller and forwarded to State Department officials.
subfiles.from: Francis P. Miller
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes a letter dated December 23, 1933, from Francis P. Miller enclosing notes on Japan sent to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck and Assistant Secretary R. Walton Moore.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 893.00/12656 (Notes on Japan by Francis P. Miller)
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and R. Walton Moore

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum commenting on Paris Special Report No. W.D. 1363 regarding articles in Le Temps.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (SK)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum critiques the assertion by French journalist Chevallier that Japan enjoyed an uninterrupted decade of prosperity prior to the current crisis. It notes that severe depression struck Japan in 1920 and persisted until 1932, serving as a contributing cause of the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Le Temps Articles Regarding Japan's Economic and Political Conditions

subfiles.about: Special Report transmitting and summarizing articles from the French newspaper Le Temps analyzing Japan's political and social crisis.
subfiles.from: Jesse Isidor Straus / Warrington Dawson, Paris
subfiles.summary: Warrington Dawson forwards articles by F. Chevallier discussing Japan's political evolution, constitutional framework, parliamentary corruption, and the military's resurgence since the 1931 Mukden incident. The enclosed clippings examine the historical divergence between Western parliamentary democracy and Japanese imperial and samurai traditions.
subfiles.title: Special Report No. W.D. 1363: Correspondence of Le Temps From The Far East

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum recommending the reading of Tokyo Despatch No. 656 regarding Consul General Davis's interview in Chosen.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (EHD / REK)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs draws attention to Despatch No. 656, which records statements made by the Japanese commanding general in Chosen to American Consul General Davis.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 656

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on a farewell interview between Consul General Davis of Seoul and Lieutenant General Kawashima.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Consul General Davis reports that Lieutenant General Kawashima spoke enthusiastically of Japan's progress in civilization and hoped that the peoples of Manchuria, China, and Siberia would soon share these benefits. Grew observes that Kawashima's statements exemplify the mindset of the Japanese military.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 656: Farewell Interview of Consul General Davis of Seoul with Lieutenant General Kawashima

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 683 on political attacks against the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (FE: EHD: ABW)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Grew's report on Diet attacks against the Saito Cabinet and internal dissensions in the Seiyukai Party. It emphasizes the Embassy's conclusion that the government possesses sufficient resilience to withstand current political challenges.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 683 Regarding the Position of the Saito Government
subfiles.to: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on political attacks against the Saito Cabinet in the Diet, financial scandals, and a discussion with Saburo Kurusu.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The despatch examines Diet attacks against Baron Nakajima and Education Minister Hatoyama, alongside controversies involving Bank of Taiwan share sales and steel mergers. An enclosed memorandum of conversation between Edwin L. Neville and Saburo Kurusu indicates that the public distrusts political parties and expects Prime Minister Saito to weather the political crisis.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 683: The Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum commenting on Tokyo Despatch No. 685 regarding the May 15 incident civilian trials.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (EHD: EJL)
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights the severe sentences handed down to civilian conspirators compared to military and naval officers convicted in the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai. It notes that public perception of this leniency toward military personnel is contributing to discontent with military dominance.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 685 Regarding Reactionary Trials

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an instalment of the report on the trials of twenty civilians involved in the May 15, 1932 Incident and notes the February 1934 imperial amnesty.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The despatch and attached report describe the court proceedings against twenty civilians led by Kozaburo Tachibana and Dr. Shumei Okawa who attempted to bomb electric transformer stations in Tokyo during the May 15, 1932 Incident. It details Tachibana's agrarian testimony advocating direct imperial rule, the heavy prison sentences imposed by the civilian court, and their subsequent partial commutation under the Imperial Amnesty of February 11, 1934.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 685: Report on the Trials of the Reactionaries Involved in the Incident of May 15, 1932
